baseline_incident_edges.relationship: investigates domestic service and household work before postwar expansion
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. Original preface and chapters I–II support the concrete labor inquiry; the 1906 Apologia distinguishes its purpose from household panaceas. Evidence limits and acknowledged collective work remain explicit.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: offers earlier investigations of ordinary life and social evidence
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The Vassar account uses social-history terminology retrospectively; this link does not move Salmon into a school that expanded after her death. The primary opening connects household work with industrial change, while the preface discusses nonresponse. This is an earlier comparison, not postwar movement membership.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: invites comparison through cookbooks, household objects, and everyday evidence
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: A comparison of evidence and questions, not a direct genealogy from Salmon to the 1980s consumption-history literature. The original chapters consider changing household production; Vassar documents material-source pedagogy. Neither establishes a direct genealogy of the later consumption movement.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: shares critical work with sources while extending the range of evidence and subjects
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Not an assertion that her pedagogy derived solely from Ranke; source criticism and social inquiry can coexist. Salmon’s Apologia explicitly names Tyler’s instruction on judging a work’s purpose. This adds a specific interlocutor without reclassifying the existing Ranke comparison as influence.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Salmon combines employer and worker questionnaires with statistical comparisons and discussion of nonresponse
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Original preface explains network distribution, respondent hesitations and comparative tabulation. This is earlier quantitative practice; no general influence on later cliometrics or independent validation of the tables is claimed.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The staple approach as a Canadian contribution to economic history
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Watkins (1963): the staple approach "is primarily a Canadian innovation; indeed, it is Canada's most distinctive contribution to political economy", with Innis as "the leading innovator". Salmon (1997): the staple thesis gave "an economic rationale for Canadian political development". Contribution to the field, not a claim that economic history adopted it generally. The atlas economic entry has no Canadian anchors, so no PhD overlap is computed.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The staple studies: Canada read through its exports of fur and fish (1930, 1940)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Innis's own statement, 1930 conclusion (pp. 386–397 read): 'The economic history of Canada has been dominated by the discrepancy between the center and the margin of western civilization. Energy has been directed toward the exploitation of staple products and the tendency has been cumulative' (p. 388); 'The northern half of North America remained British because of the importance of fur as a staple product' (p. 396); 'The present Dominion emerged not in spite of geography but because of it' (p. 397). Watkins (1963, opening paragraphs read) calls him 'the leading innovator' whose work 'stamped the “school”', with an approach 'more technological history writ large than a theory of economic growth'. Brady (1953, read in full) traces his study of 'the staple industries, beginning with the fur trade and fisheries' (p. 89). Salmon (1997, pp. 180–181 read): the staple thesis 'provided an economic rationale for Canadian political development'. A contribution, not a founding: Watkins says 'others tilled the same vineyard', Salmon notes that 'Innis never claimed to have originated the staples theory' (n. 2), Brady calls Adam Shortt 'the pioneer in these economic studies' (p. 91), and Mackintosh's 1923 article precedes the book. The Cod Fisheries is checked at catalogue level only. In the sampled corpus, 82 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite any of his works; the citation share falls from 7.1% (2009–14) and 6.8% (2015–19) to 4.9% (2020–26). Of the 82, 48 cite The Fur Trade in Canada and 6 The Cod Fisheries. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Environmental change through land use, subsistence and labour: Island County (1980), the roots of Native dependency (1983) and the Columbia as an organic machine (1995), with an early survey of the field (1985)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: White's own statements, known for his books only through Google Books search-within snippets (page images not seen) and therefore paraphrased where the wording carries the claim. Land Use, Environment, and Social Change (1980; snippets of the 1992 paperback, whose body text is the 1980 text; p. 7 as given in the snippet results): White presents the book as departing somewhat from recent environmental history, which he describes as mostly a variant of intellectual and political history, by tracing the environmental impact of Indian and later intruding peoples and its consequences for their societies; on the same page he credits James Malin's Great Plains studies, ignored by most historians, as a trail to follow. In the preface to the 1992 edition (November 1991; snippet, folio xviii inferred from Google Books page ids that carry the printed folios xi, xvi and xvii) he judges his own use of ecology: 'I used ecological concepts like community, succession, climax, and ecosystem unproblematically even though within the discipline of ecology those ideas had already come under attack'. Cronon's foreword (October 1991; snippets, folio xi observed) places the book among White's contributions 'to environmental history, to the history of the American West, to Indian history, and to American history generally' and calls it 'a textbook case of an underappreciated classic' (p. xi). The Organic Machine (1995; snippets of the preface, whose printed folios were not visible, and of the conclusion, p. 112 taken from the Google Books page id, not seen as a printed folio), in paraphrase: White examines the Columbia as an organic machine, an energy system modified by human intervention that keeps natural, unmade qualities; human labour is energy as much as the river's flow or the calories salmon store for their journey; environmentalists, he argues, distance humans from nature by favouring the eye over the hand and contemplation over work; and the conclusion finds the nature in us in our labour and energy (p. 112). In-period third-party readings: Cronon (1993; OCR of the author-hosted page scan) footnotes Land Use and The Roots of Dependency (nn. 15, 23) for the lesson that 'the horse was not simply a European invader, but a complex cultural entity' (p. 9); D. R. Miller (1994; PDF read in full) calls him 'The social and environmental historian Richard White' (p. 157) and quotes The Middle Ground that dependency 'is an economic, political, and social relationship, but can also be an environmental relationship' (p. 169). On the 1985 survey (unread; paywalled): Worster (1990, read in the 2002–03 Portuguese translation, n. 5, p. 42) calls it the best effort to trace the field's emergence, 'pelo menos em uma parte influente do mundo', reporting White's view that frontier and western history was the formative influence; Cronon's 1994 graduate syllabus assigns it 'read for main themes' (p. 4); in Canada, Cook (1990) cites it (n. 4) for Turner and Webb as 'important, if declining, influences into the 1950s' (p. 6). A contribution, not a founding. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013) names White among historians who 'synthesized the material and cultural approaches to the environment' (p. 87) and quotes his 1990 round-table objection that Worster's scheme reduced culture to 'superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense' (pp. 88–89, citing JAH 76, pp. 1112–1113; the JAH text is unread).
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Land use, labour and the field, 1980–1995

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The Laurentian narrative: the St. Lawrence commercial system as the basis of a transcontinental Canada (1937), carried through Dominion of the North (1944) and the Macdonald biography (1952–55)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, his own text. Dominion of the North (1944; pages read in an open copy): the post at Quebec gave the French 'the one great river system which led to the Atlantic seaboard from the heart of the continent'; 'Inevitably the river came to seem the natural basis of a great commercial empire stretching far into the distant west; and the achievement of this empire became the common objective of successive generations of Canadians, though their methods altered and the staple products of their trade were sometimes changed. The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur' (p. 21); the rivalry of 'the northern and southern routes, between Montreal and New York, for the control of the Great Lakes system and the command of the western trade', a conflict that 'was to remain essentially the same' (pp. 24–25); 'Quebec had been the origin of the empire of the St. Lawrence; it was to be the genesis of the Dominion of Canada' (p. 298). In-period reception. Herbert Heaton's review (CJEPS, 1938; first page, p. 565, read) quotes the book as 'an attempt to trace the relations between the commercial system of the St. Lawrence and the political development of Canada' (the book's words as Heaton quotes them; the 1937 book is unread) and reads it as a test of the economic interpretation of history that 'has pleased neither the Marxians nor their enemies'. Michel Brunet (RHAF, 1953, p. 579) calls him 'l'un des maîtres contemporains de l'historiographie anglo-canadienne'; Guy Frégault (RHAF, 1955, p. 446) sums up the Macdonald biography as 'Nationalisme antiaméricain, impérialisme et centralisation : synthèse canadienne, — je veux dire anglo-canadienne'. His own retrospect, 1969 (read in full; a later statement by the author, not evidence of what the 1937 book says): 'This Laurentian theme has its basis in the fact that the St. Lawrence is the one great river system that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent of North America'; the river 'has inspired generations of Canadians to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior of the continent' (p. 16); 'The west, it was believed, would make Canada a nation, and the east-west axis would be its backbone' (p. 17); in choosing Macdonald he had 'stumbled upon the only satisfactory method of writing the second phase', so that he had written 'a trilogy on one theme' (p. 16). The phrase, he says, came to be regarded 'as the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school of Canadian historians and as the genesis of a new historical doctrine, the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history'; he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea' (p. 14). Later readings: Ouellet (1984, pp. 226–227) calls him 'le chef de l'Ecole laurentienne'; Salmon (1997) says he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. Contested in period: Brunet found French-Canadian newspapers unread ('Il n'a pas jugé nécessaire de dépouiller un seul journal canadien-français', p. 580) and 'nombreux préjugés' (p. 581); Frégault asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ? Tout simplement, ils n'y sont pas' (p. 447), while praising the work as 'fondé sur une compréhension exacte de l'histoire du Canada' (p. 444); W. L. Morton, as quoted by Davis (1985), saw in Creighton 'the preponderant role commercial monopoly and centralized business have played' (Davis, p. 97) and held that the metropolitan thesis, which he associated with Creighton and Careless, 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (Davis, p. 98); the critic George Woodcock (1979, p. 140) called his treatment of Confederation as centralist 'a major distortion'. A contribution, not a founding.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Innis's staple studies as a resource for Creighton's Laurentian narrative, as Creighton's own staple vocabulary and later readers show; Creighton rejected the story that the 1937 book grew from their friendship
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own texts. Dominion of the North (1944) frames the St. Lawrence system by its staples ('The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur', p. 21), and its reading list (pp. 505–507) names Innis's The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) and The Cod Fisheries (1940). The 1957 presidential address recalls 'the 1930's, when the influence of Harold Innis was at its height and everybody was writing and talking about staple production' (p. 3), and exempts Innis from the Marxian fashion: 'most of the professional economists — and especially Innis — refused to accept the simplified Marxian version of historical determinism' (p. 6). In 1957 he also published Harold Adams Innis: Portrait of a Scholar (unread); Benoît Brouillette's review (1957, p. 529, read) reports Creighton's account of Innis's Canada as an east–west system 'marqué par le Saint-Laurent et les Grands-Lacs', at once 'transocéanique et transcontinental'. The qualification, his own (1969, pp. 14–15): 'The Empire of the St. Lawrence, it is sometimes confidently asserted, was the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis ... These explanations, like most simple generalizations, happen to be wrong'; the subject was suggested 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time, but by W. P. M. Kennedy', and he was 'reluctantly convinced by the weight of his own evidence' about the Montreal merchants (p. 16). Readers: George Woodcock (1979, p. 134): 'Creighton's master was H. A. Innis, especially the Innis of The Fur Trade in Canada, which contained the essential germ out of which — with Innis's encouragement — Creighton built the scenario of his first book'; Fernand Ouellet (1984, p. 226): Creighton started 'partant de la théorie des staples'; Deborah Harrison (1981), as quoted by Davis (1985, p. 97): 'probably the first to advance a metropolitanist interpretation, although the closely related "staples" thesis had been put forward by Innis much earlier'; Salmon (1997): he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. The edge records Innis's work as a resource the Laurentian narrative used, not a teacher–pupil derivation; Creighton's denial concerns the origin of the subject, not the use of the staple framework.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Staples behind the Laurentian narrative, contested
